title: Gossip

jokes.text: Michael, Dwight, and Andy shouting 'Parkour!' while running through the office parking lot like children
jokes.setup: Parkour is a legitimate athletic discipline requiring skill and training
jokes.punchline: Three middle-aged office workers scream the word while doing rudimentary jumps over boxes and each other in a parking lot, treating the label as a substitute for the skill
jokes.explanation: A superb cold open built entirely on character. Michael's childlike enthusiasm for trends years after their peak is deeply in-character, and the physicality (grown men shouting a single word while leaping over mundane objects) is a strong visual gag. The joke is sustained through escalation and the participants' total sincerity.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'So technically they are doing parkour, as long as point A is delusion and point B is the hospital.'
jokes.setup: Jim explains parkour's legitimate premise — getting from point A to point B as creatively as possible
jokes.punchline: Redefines the points as 'delusion' and 'the hospital,' perfectly summarizing the absurdity in one line
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The structure is airtight: Jim sincerely repeats the parkour definition, then uses the same grammatical frame to obliterate it. The economy is exceptional — the joke does three things simultaneously (lampshades the cold open, characterizes Michael and the others as delusional, and positions Jim as the audience surrogate) in a single clause. Highly quotable, perfectly in Jim's deadpan voice. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft quality.

jokes.text: Visual gag: The parkour sequence continues with Michael calling for 'Truck to refrigerators to dumpster, 360 spin onto the palettes, back flip, gainer into the trashcan' — an absurdly elaborate plan none of them can execute
jokes.setup: The trio has been doing very simple jumps and calling it parkour
jokes.punchline: Michael narrates an impossibly complex sequence as if they are about to execute it, revealing the total gap between their ambition and ability
jokes.explanation: Effective escalation of the cold open joke. Michael's deadpan announcement of a stunt sequence — 'gainer' — that these three men will obviously not land amplifies the absurdity. Works as a payoff beat within the parkour cold open.

jokes.text: Cut to: one of them (likely Michael or Andy) lying on the ground after the attempt, with a single understated 'Parkour.'
jokes.setup: The elaborate stunt sequence was announced with great bravado
jokes.punchline: A single defeated 'Parkour' delivered from the ground implies total failure without showing it — the word itself becomes the punchline
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in comedic economy. The single whispered 'Parkour' after the failed stunt is the perfect button to the cold open — the word that started as triumphant now functions as a defeated sigh. Maximum funny per word; the audience fills in the physical disaster themselves.

jokes.text: Michael tells the intern to put files in random order and then come back for an 'assignment concerning their order'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving the intern a meaningful task on their last day
jokes.punchline: The task is deliberately pointless — randomizing files only so they can be fixed — revealing Michael's obliviousness to management and his need to seem important
jokes.explanation: Solid character joke revealing Michael's incompetence as a manager — he creates busywork that is circular by design. Functional but not a standout; this kind of Michael-is-a-bad-boss gag is well-trodden territory.

jokes.text: Talking head explanation of why the internship program was shut down: 'Ever since Michael's Monica Lewinsky incident. He didn't do anything sexual. He just made far, far too many Monica Lewinsky jokes.'
jokes.setup: The phrase 'Monica Lewinsky incident' implies something scandalous and sexual
jokes.punchline: The incident was only that Michael made too many Monica Lewinsky jokes — a perfectly Michael-scale scandal that is both embarrassing and completely non-sexual
jokes.explanation: Sharp misdirect with strong character integration. 'Monica Lewinsky incident' primes the audience for genuine misconduct; the reveal that he simply made too many jokes is both a relief and a perfect summation of Michael's pathology — he offends through sheer oblivious excess, not malice. The phrase 'far, far too many' does great work.

jokes.text: Kevin speculates that the two interns might hook up: 'Think she did him? I bet there's something there.'
jokes.setup: Colleagues are discussing the last day of summer interns
jokes.punchline: Kevin immediately and crudely sexualizes the professional relationship with the unfiltered candor he is known for
jokes.explanation: Functionally in-character for Kevin but not especially crafted. The joke relies entirely on Kevin's established filter-free persona. Gets mild recognition laughs but nothing more.

jokes.text: 'This place is like Spaniard fly.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is trying to say this office is like an aphrodisiac ('Spanish fly')
jokes.punchline: Kevin says 'Spaniard fly' — a malapropism that is somehow both wrong and funnier than the original
jokes.explanation: A great Kevin malapropism. 'Spaniard fly' is the perfect wrong word — it sounds like something a person might say if they half-remembered 'Spanish fly,' and 'Spaniard' adds an unintentionally formal, almost Shakespearean quality. Strong character integration because only Kevin would use this word.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam's talking head about keeping the pregnancy secret, with Jim doing air quotes on 'knocked up by some guy'
jokes.setup: They explain why they're not announcing the pregnancy — office gossips would spin it
jokes.punchline: Pam describes her own situation from the perspective of the office gossips: 'unmarried, knocked up by some guy' — Jim is that guy
jokes.explanation: Competent situational irony — Pam narrates her own situation in the third-person gossip voice. Gets the point across efficiently but doesn't reach for anything exceptional.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Wait, there's not going to be a shotgun?' / Pam: 'Nope.' / Jim: 'No shotgun? Because that changes everything.'
jokes.setup: Pam explains they don't want people thinking Jim is being 'marched down the aisle with a shotgun'
jokes.punchline: Jim feigns that the absence of a shotgun makes the wedding optional, threatening to back out — Pam calls his bluff
jokes.explanation: Sweet character beat between Jim and Pam that doubles as a joke. Jim's faux-serious 'that changes everything' plays on the shotgun wedding trope and reveals their relaxed dynamic. Works because it's earned through seasons of their relationship.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Free at last, free at last.' / Pam: 'No, keep it up. You'll never guess what I know.'
jokes.setup: Jim jokes about being 'free' without a shotgun forcing the wedding
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately dangles a secret to reel him back in, using information as leverage
jokes.explanation: Functional transition joke. Jim's MLK reference is a slightly too-big reference for the moment, but Pam's pivot to dangling gossip is a neat character beat showing how the episode's gossip plot hooks everyone.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about having 'a face you can trust' because of his 'low cheekbones'
jokes.setup: Michael explains why people tell him gossip — 'I guess I have a face you can trust'
jokes.punchline: He attributes it to his 'low cheekbones' — a completely made-up and anatomically bizarre explanation delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: A great Michael Scott absurdist moment. The logic that low cheekbones signal trustworthiness is pure nonsense delivered as genuine insight. Works because Michael's false wisdom is a cornerstone of his character — he always has a confident, wrong explanation.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional: 'I hate, hate, hate being left out. Whether it's not being picked for a team, or being picked for a team and then showing up and realizing the team doesn't exist, or that the sport doesn't exist. I should have known. Poopball?'
jokes.setup: Michael expresses his dread of being excluded
jokes.punchline: The escalation goes from normal (not being picked) to surreal (the team doesn't exist) to absurd (the sport doesn't exist) and then delivers 'Poopball' as if it were a real sport someone actually tricked him into believing in
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the finest Michael Scott confessionals in the series. The three-part escalation — normal exclusion, nonexistent team, nonexistent sport — is perfectly structured, each step more tragic than the last. Then 'Poopball?' lands as one word doing enormous comedic work: it implies he was once told a sport called Poopball existed, he believed it, showed up, and was devastated. The self-recrimination ('I should have known') is the perfect button. Exceptional character integration — no other character on any show could deliver this.

jokes.text: 'The third wheel is what makes it a tricycle.' — Michael's mom's advice
jokes.setup: Michael says he's been 'the third wheel so many times' and that his mom told him something that made him feel better
jokes.punchline: His mom's comforting wisdom is 'The third wheel is what makes it a tricycle' — a statement that sounds wise but is both anatomically incorrect (tricycles have three wheels, all equal) and philosophically meaningless as consolation
jokes.explanation: A wonderful piece of false wisdom. It sounds inspirational for approximately half a second before you realize it doesn't hold up — a tricycle's third wheel isn't a spare, it's structural, which makes the metaphor accidentally correct in the wrong way. The joke works on multiple levels: it characterizes Michael's mom as equally oblivious, and it shows Michael has internalized bad advice as genuine wisdom. High quotability.

jokes.text: Michael reveals he knows about the intern group date from seeing Stanley at the club — but Stanley was with his mistress, not his wife
jokes.setup: Michael casually reveals he knows about the intern group date at Tinks, leading them to ask how he knew
jokes.punchline: His source is Stanley, whom he saw at the same club — but Stanley was there with his mistress, which Michael doesn't yet realize
jokes.explanation: A well-structured dramatic irony setup — Michael doesn't know what he's stumbled into. The rewatch value is high because once you know the Stanley affair plotline, this scene becomes richer. As a first-watch joke it's more of a plot mechanism than a pure laugh.

jokes.text: Michael says 'I waved at him but he didn't wave back' about Stanley — a moment of comedic obliviousness, then 'There he goes.' as Michael immediately goes to spread the gossip
jokes.setup: Michael has just realized Stanley was at a nightclub with someone who wasn't his wife
jokes.punchline: The audience (and Jim) watches Michael's face process this and then immediately march off to spread the news — 'There he goes' is Jim's deadpan reaction shot
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'There he goes' is a tiny gem of reaction comedy. Two words summarize Michael's entire personality: he cannot resist gossip, the audience knows it, Jim knows it, and those three words confirm it all. Strong economy score.

jokes.text: Michael gossips that Stanley is having a midlife crisis and was 'at a club for young people.' Oscar immediately counters: 'Stanley is way past the middle of his life, especially considering his height-to-weight ratio.'
jokes.setup: Michael is spreading gossip about Stanley's supposed midlife crisis
jokes.punchline: Oscar flatly points out that Stanley's health means he's mathematically past the midpoint of his life — framing a harsh observation about mortality as a logical counter-argument
jokes.explanation: Oscar's dry, analytical cruelty is perfectly in character. He doesn't deliver it as an insult — he delivers it as a factual correction, which makes it darker and funnier. 'Height-to-weight ratio' is the specific detail that elevates it from a generic fat joke to an Oscar-specific dissection.

jokes.text: Michael confronts Jim: 'You stupid son of a bitch. You set me up.' — realizing Jim told him false info about Stanley's wife being away
jokes.setup: Michael discovers that Stanley's wife was actually out of town — meaning Stanley was at the club with someone else
jokes.punchline: Michael blames Jim for 'setting him up' by telling the truth — the irony being that accurate information accidentally exposed Stanley's affair
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Michael's logic is inverted (he accuses Jim of a setup when Jim just stated facts). Functional situational comedy.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I don't get it! If that was his sister, then what they were doing was totally illegal.' Jim: 'Drugs?' Michael: 'Making out.'
jokes.setup: Michael speculates whether the woman Stanley was with could have been his sister
jokes.punchline: The 'illegal' activity Michael was imagining is incest — but Jim assumes it would be drugs, a gap that itself reveals both their worldviews
jokes.explanation: Excellent two-beat joke. The structure is nearly perfect: Michael says something that could mean several illegal things, Jim takes a logical guess (drugs), and Michael's 'Making out' reveals his mind went straight to incest — which is simultaneously more disturbing and more absurd than drugs. Economy is superb; three words deliver the punchline.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about the joy of having people's attention when sharing gossip: 'When you have somebody's attention and their eyes are lighting up... that is a great feeling.'
jokes.setup: Michael reflects on the pleasure of sharing information
jokes.punchline: What he describes as a meaningful human connection is simply the thrill of gossip — the emotional insight is real but applied to something shallow, exposing Michael's arrested development
jokes.explanation: A softer character joke that humanizes Michael's gossip addiction without landing a specific punchline. More of a thematic beat than a laugh.

jokes.text: Michael helping an intern with a crossword: 'Q.' / 'No.' / intern staring / 'He's holding a pencil. He could be doing a crossword puzzle with that pencil.' / Eventually gets to 'T! Yes! T!' — Michael cannot identify the letter T
jokes.setup: Michael is helping an intern in what appears to be a mentorship moment
jokes.punchline: Michael cannot identify the letter T in a word, confidently guessing Q, and then celebrates 'T!' as if it's a breakthrough — suggesting he may be functionally illiterate or just profoundly oblivious
jokes.explanation: Effective cringe-comedy. The crossword bit plays on Michael's performative mentorship that masks fundamental incompetence. 'You're almost there' — said to an intern who correctly identified a letter — is a nice button showing Michael's total lack of self-awareness.

jokes.text: Michael stops Stanley to interrogate him with: 'I'm casting a movie and I'm looking for a woman who can dance, beautiful woman. Do you know anybody?' / Stanley: 'Goodbye.' / Michael: 'Pays 5 million dollars. Nudity required.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to probe Stanley about his affair without being direct
jokes.punchline: His chosen method of inquiry is posing as a movie casting agent — an implausible cover story that immediately collapses, then he escalates with 'Nudity required' as Stanley walks away
jokes.explanation: Michael's espionage strategy being a terrible movie-casting lie is very funny, and 'Nudity required' as a parting shot to Stanley's retreating back is a good absurdist escalation. Strong character integration — Michael's schemes are always this transparently bad.

jokes.text: Jim confronts Michael: 'Okay. I get it. You feel out of the loop and you feel sorry for yourself, and it's really sad because everybody thinks you're a loser.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to get Michael to stop spreading the Stanley affair rumor
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'comfort' speech begins reasonably but pivots to 'everybody thinks you're a loser' — delivered as if this is just a neutral fact Jim is passing along
jokes.explanation: Jim's brutally honest assessment packaged as empathy is funny. The joke is in how Jim slides from sympathetic language to blunt diagnosis without seeming to notice the shift.

jokes.text: Jim confronts Michael about spreading gossip: 'Everybody thinks you're a loser... you might be ruining his life.' Then immediately: 'Hold up! Hold up! No, no, no!' — Michael publicly confronts Stanley
jokes.setup: Jim gives Michael a serious talking-to about the consequences of spreading unverified gossip
jokes.punchline: Michael appears to have been convinced — for approximately five seconds — before immediately calling Stanley out in front of everyone
jokes.explanation: The speed of Michael's reversal after appearing chastened is the joke. The very brief pause between Jim's lecture and Michael's 'Hold up! Hold up!' is a perfect cringe beat. Classic Michael Scott — he understands consequences in theory but cannot apply that understanding.

jokes.text: Stanley, after being publicly confronted, claims it was 'racial profiling gossip' — then immediately pivots: 'Damn! I told her it was a stupid idea to go up in that club.'
jokes.setup: Stanley denies the affair claim as 'racial profiling gossip'
jokes.punchline: One breath later, he abandons the denial entirely and confirms the affair with 'Damn! I told her...' — his own immediate self-incrimination is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured joke. The denial-then-immediate-self-incrimination is a classic comedic pattern executed with great economy. 'Racial profiling gossip' is a notably specific (and slightly deflective) phrase that gets a laugh on its own, making the reversal even sharper.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'We used to go on these long walks on the treadmill.' — describing his romantic connection with his mistress
jokes.setup: Stanley is explaining how his relationship with Cynthia began romantically during rehabilitation
jokes.punchline: 'Long walks on the treadmill' — the romantic cliché of long walks deflated by the word 'treadmill,' which is both medically accurate and hilariously anti-romantic
jokes.explanation: A genuinely exceptional joke. The phrase weaponizes the romantic cliché 'long walks' by appending 'on the treadmill' — a single word that transforms a romantic notion into something simultaneously sad, specific, and funny. It's perfect economy: five words, maximum comedy. Also perfectly character-integrated — Stanley's earnest, flat delivery makes the absurdity land harder. One of the episode's very best lines. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Michael, after learning about Stanley's affair: 'Wait, wait, wait. Do people often say they're going on sales calls and then go someplace else? Because that's not cool.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just discovered Stanley was lying about sales calls to cover for meeting his mistress
jokes.punchline: Michael's reaction is not moral outrage about the affair — it's concern about the integrity of the sales-call alibi as a business practice
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Michael Scott priority-inversion joke. He's just learned his employee has been having an affair, and his primary concern is whether the 'sales call' excuse undermines workplace accountability. 'Because that's not cool' is the perfect flat button. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'She apparently is dating an 81-year-old billionaire. Owns a Quiznos on the turnpike.'
jokes.setup: Michael is inventing false gossip to spread in order to muddy the waters around the Stanley affair
jokes.punchline: He describes Angela's supposed boyfriend as an '81-year-old billionaire' — then immediately undercuts 'billionaire' with 'Owns a Quiznos on the turnpike'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. The structure is a classic inflate-deflate: 'billionaire' is impressive, then 'Owns a Quiznos on the turnpike' immediately reveals that Michael's idea of a billionaire is someone who owns a single fast-food franchise. The specificity of 'on the turnpike' is crucial — it makes it a real, sad, perfectly imagined place. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head strategy: 'How do you un-tell something? You can't. What you can do is spread false gossip, so that people think that everything that's been said is untrue, including "Stanley is having an affair." It's like the end of Spartacus.'
jokes.setup: Michael needs to retract the Stanley affair gossip without admitting he spread it
jokes.punchline: His solution is to spread MORE false gossip to create confusion, and he references Spartacus as a strategic precedent — while also revealing he thinks Spartacus is a mystery film ('classic whodunit')
jokes.explanation: Strong Michael Scott logic joke. The plan is terrible (fighting gossip with more gossip). The Spartacus reference is doubly funny because: (a) he uses it incorrectly as a strategic analogy and (b) he's seen it 'half a dozen times' and still doesn't understand the plot, calling it a 'classic whodunit.' His utter confidence in this flawed analysis is peak Michael.

jokes.text: Michael's gossip montage: 'Kelly has an eating disorder.' / 'Yes.' / 'She always eats my lunch.' / 'Anorexia.' / 'She's an anorexitic.'
jokes.setup: Michael is spreading false rumors to confuse people about which gossip is true
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'evidence' for Kelly's anorexia is that she eats his lunch, and he invents the word 'anorexitic' — the wrong diagnosis compounded by a made-up word
jokes.explanation: The Kelly anorexia gossip is funny on two levels: the backwards logic (anorexia = eats too much in Michael's world) and 'anorexitic' as a confident malapropism. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael gossip montage continues: 'I'm worried about Erin because she's not a very good worker.' / 'And Andy is gay.' / 'Did you hear Pam is pregnant?' / 'She's going to hate being a mom.'
jokes.setup: Michael is spraying false gossip in rapid succession to obscure the Stanley truth
jokes.punchline: The montage of Michael's gossip accelerates — some plausible, some absurd, some accidentally true (Pam is pregnant) — the escalation and variety of targets is the joke
jokes.explanation: The montage format works well; rapid-fire delivery gives it energy. The rewatch value is high because knowing Pam IS pregnant makes 'Did you hear Pam is pregnant?' — delivered as invented gossip — ironic. 'She's going to hate being a mom' is an unnecessarily harsh add-on that gets a surprised laugh.

jokes.text: Two office workers discussing Andy's rumored gayness via a prolonged tea metaphor: 'Do you like it as much as you like men's butts? Because you're gay.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has heard that Andy is gay and is confronting him indirectly through questions about his tea preference
jokes.punchline: Kevin abandons all subtlety and just says 'Because you're gay' — the extended tea metaphor was unnecessary and Kevin knew it
jokes.explanation: Functionally in-character for Kevin (he can't sustain a metaphor) and the tea setup is a decent lead-in. But the punchline itself is blunt to the point of just being a statement. Gets a laugh from the tonal whiplash.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'Was it Broccoli Rob? Someone from Chi Psi? Or did you run into someone from my high school? This is not the first time rumors about me being gay have come up. Twice before, actually. Just a weird coincidence.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to figure out the source of the gay rumor
jokes.punchline: Instead of denying being gay, he lists all the possible sources — Broccoli Rob, Chi Psi, his high school — revealing that in every social circle he's been in, someone has spread this rumor; then calls it 'just a weird coincidence'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is superb: each new named source (Broccoli Rob — a perfect absurd name — Chi Psi, high school) is a new wave of evidence against Andy's heterosexuality, and his inability to see what the pattern means is the punchline. 'Just a weird coincidence' is a perfect closer. The character integration is exceptional — Andy's oblivious self-justification is his defining trait. 'Broccoli Rob' alone is a comedy achievement.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head continues: 'Almost makes you wonder if it's not a coincidence at all. Whoa! Which it is, of course. But it makes you wonder.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just acknowledged the pattern of gay rumors following him through life
jokes.punchline: He nearly has a genuine moment of self-realization ('Whoa!') then immediately retreats: 'Which it is, of course.' The 'Whoa!' is the joke — the audience sees him touch the truth and pull away
jokes.explanation: The immediate self-correction ('Which it is, of course. But it makes you wonder.') is beautifully structured. Andy's 'Whoa!' functions as a near-breakthrough for a character who has built walls so high he can't see over them. The joke works because the audience is ahead of Andy — his near-miss with self-awareness is both funny and poignant. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Andy asks Oscar if he thinks the gay rumor is true. Oscar: 'Are you attracted to other men?' Andy: 'No. But let me kick you a scenario...' — the Brad Pitt beach cabana fantasy
jokes.setup: Andy is asking Oscar (the office's openly gay man) to evaluate whether Andy is gay
jokes.punchline: Andy's denial immediately becomes an elaborately detailed fantasy about resisting Brad Pitt 'at first' at a beach cabana — each new detail making his heterosexuality less convincing
jokes.explanation: A genuinely exceptional extended joke. The escalation is perfect: Andy says 'No' (simple denial), then immediately qualifies with a fantasy about resisting Brad Pitt, then adds 'at first,' then 'if he was persistent I might give in a little,' then 'how hard would I push him away? What if he's really aggressive?' Each clause is funnier than the last and more incriminating. The structure is impeccable — it's a sustained cringe escalation that earns every laugh. One of the episode's top-tier moments.

jokes.text: Oscar's talking head: 'What exactly is my responsibility here? To comfort insecure heterosexual men? That can't possibly fall to me.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has just had to navigate Andy's elaborate Brad Pitt fantasy while Andy looked to him for answers
jokes.punchline: Oscar's exasperated deadpan breaks the fourth wall of his role as the office's gay man — he refuses the responsibility of being everyone's sexuality consultant
jokes.explanation: Oscar's reaction confessional is perfectly calibrated. 'That can't possibly fall to me' is an extremely quotable line that works because it's both specific to the situation and universally relatable. High character integration — Oscar's dry, slightly weary dignity is his signature register, and this expresses it perfectly.

jokes.text: Michael's intern send-off speech: 'Look to the intern on your left. Now to your right. One of you will do exceedingly well in business, unlimited potential. One of you will make a living and nothing more. And one of you will make a great mother.'
jokes.setup: Michael is delivering a grand, inspirational send-off speech to three interns in the style of a commencement address
jokes.punchline: The classic 'look left, look right' speech pattern requires two outcomes for three people — Michael adds a third outcome, 'make a great mother,' which is both patronizing to whoever he's directing it at and reveals he can't count
jokes.explanation: A great subversion of the classic motivational speech template. The pattern sets up two outcomes (left/right), Michael adds an unnecessary and quietly sexist third ('make a great mother'), and the joke works because it simultaneously parodies commencement clichés, reveals Michael's casual sexism, and exposes that he doesn't understand the 'look left/right' format which only requires two fates. Sharp structure.

jokes.text: Michael gives interns his business card: 'Call me any time of the day or night.' Intern: 'Why would we call you at night?' Michael: 'Well, now you can't call me at all, so problem solved.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving a generous, open invitation to call him at any hour
jokes.punchline: When an intern questions the 'at night' part, Michael punishes all of them by revoking the offer entirely — a petulant reversal that reveals his fragile ego
jokes.explanation: Good Michael joke. His immediate pivot from 'anytime' to 'now you can't call at all' over one mild question is a perfect expression of his emotional immaturity. 'Problem solved' as a self-satisfied button works well.

jokes.text: Michael follow-up to intern: 'You're going to regret that when you find yourself between a moose and her cubs at night.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just revoked his offer to be called at night
jokes.punchline: He immediately justifies the offer's value with a completely random wilderness emergency scenario — a moose and her cubs — as if this is a plausible situation an office intern might face
jokes.explanation: The moose scenario is a perfect non-sequitur that reveals Michael's self-image as a survivalist mentor. 'Between a moose and her cubs at night' is specific enough to be very funny — it's not just 'danger,' it's a very particular, very wildlife-documentary-specific situation. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Michael, having spread the eating-disorder rumor about Kelly, says to her face: 'I am so happy you're eating again.'
jokes.setup: Michael invented a false eating disorder rumor about Kelly as gossip cover
jokes.punchline: He now performs concern about her 'recovery' to her face, fully inhabiting the lie he created, while Kelly has no idea what's happening
jokes.explanation: Good callback joke. The punchline is Michael's utter commitment to the bit — he's not just spreading rumors, he's now role-playing caring about Kelly's wellbeing based on a lie he invented. The cringe is potent.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head at lunch: Andy asks Jim to set him up. Jim says Pam might have friends. Andy: 'Women friends? Not guy friends? Are you interested in her guy friends?' Andy: 'No. I mean for the record I prefer women. But off the record I'm kind of confused.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Jim to set him up with someone, seemingly to prove he's straight
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'for the record / off the record' split — confidently stating he prefers women, then immediately hedging with 'kind of confused' — shows he still can't commit to a position even when trying to assert one
jokes.explanation: Solid continuation of the Andy-sexuality subplot. 'For the record / off the record' is a nice structural device. The immediate reversal is funny and consistent with Andy's character-episode-arc.

jokes.text: Jim advises Andy to figure out his sexuality by having sex with 'a woman. And then a man. And then compare.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Jim how to figure out his sexuality
jokes.punchline: Jim offers the most clinical, deadpan, almost survey-methodology approach imaginable: sample both, compare results
jokes.explanation: Jim's advice lands because of its complete lack of affect — he treats the question as a straightforward problem with an obvious solution. The pause between 'a woman' and 'And then a man' is where the joke lives. Great economy.

jokes.text: Dwight confronts Jim about the pregnancy: 'You know, a baby conceived out of wedlock is still a bastard.' Jim: 'What?' Dwight: 'Want me to say it again?'
jokes.setup: Dwight is congratulating Jim and Pam, in his way
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'congratulations' takes the form of a clinical pronouncement that their child will be a bastard — delivered without malice, purely as information — and his follow-up 'Want me to say it again?' treats Jim's shock as a hearing problem
jokes.explanation: A strong Dwight joke. 'Want me to say it again?' is the perfect button — Dwight interprets Jim's stunned 'What?' as a request for repetition, not an expression of offense. This is pure Dwight: blunt, literal, incapable of reading emotional responses. 'That can't possibly fall to me' level economy and character integration.

jokes.text: The gossip-tracing scene: 'Who's been saying that there's another person inside of me working me with controls?' — traced back through Andy, Erin, to Michael
jokes.setup: Everyone is tracing rumors back to their source, each rumor more absurd than the last
jokes.punchline: Dwight's rumor — that he is a puppet controlled by a person inside him — is so specific and so strange that it both characterizes how others see Dwight and reveals Michael's surreal imagination
jokes.explanation: The 'person inside working me with controls' rumor is a great absurdist Michael invention that's also perfect for Dwight — he's robotic enough that this rumor is almost believable, which makes it funnier. The tracing sequence is also a good structural payoff for the episode's gossip mechanics.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking head: 'Hey, did one of you tell Stanley that I have asthma? Because I don't. If it gets out they won't let me scuba. If I can't scuba, then what's this all been about? What am I working toward?'
jokes.setup: Kevin has heard a false rumor about himself and is reacting to it
jokes.punchline: Kevin's entire life purpose, apparently, is to scuba dive — and the asthma rumor threatens not just a hobby but his existential reason for working
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes and a strong contender for the standout moment. The escalation from 'I don't have asthma' to 'what am I working toward?' is perfectly paced, and the specificity of scuba as Kevin's entire life purpose is both absurd and weirdly poignant. 'If I can't scuba, then what's this all been about?' achieves a kind of accidental existential grandeur. The joke works because Kevin delivers it with complete sincerity. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Other employees revealing their false rumors: 'What do you think I'm the voice of the Taco Bell dog?' / 'How could I be a virgin? I have a daughter.'
jokes.setup: Michael's fake rumor campaign has infected the entire office with absurd false gossip
jokes.punchline: Two of Michael's invented rumors are revealed: someone is supposedly the voice of the Taco Bell chihuahua, and someone is supposedly a virgin despite having a child
jokes.explanation: Both rumors are great examples of Michael's specific brand of creativity — not plausibly damaging, just random. 'Voice of the Taco Bell dog' is an oddly specific and dated reference (perfect for Michael). 'I have a daughter, how could I be a virgin?' has perfect internal logic as a refutation. Quick escalation payoff that lands well.

jokes.text: The gossip chain traced back: 'I heard it from Andy.' 'I heard it from Erin.' 'I heard it from Michael.' Everyone turns to Michael, who tries to sneak away. 'Where are you going?' 'Nowhere.'
jokes.setup: The office traces every fake rumor back through the chain
jokes.punchline: Every single chain ends at Michael, who is caught trying to quietly disappear
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural payoff — all roads lead to Michael, who predictably tries to escape. 'Where are you going?' 'Nowhere.' is a good minimalist beat. Competent execution of an expected reveal.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'You told people that I use store-bought manure, when I showed you where my manure comes from.' — then menacing Michael with what appears to be manure-related equipment
jokes.setup: Everyone is confronting Michael about the false rumors he spread
jokes.punchline: Dwight's rumor complaint is about store-bought manure — a highly specific besmirchment of his farming authenticity — and 'when I showed you where my manure comes from' implies a genuinely horrifying memory for Michael
jokes.explanation: Only Dwight could have this complaint. The specificity of 'store-bought manure' as an insult to his beet-farming integrity is perfect character comedy. 'When I showed you where my manure comes from' suggests an experience that clearly traumatized Michael, which is funnier for remaining unshown.

jokes.text: Michael attempts to escape the confrontation by getting on the manure cart/device; everyone telling him not to: 'Don't get on it. Michael, don't. Do not. Michael, no. Michael. Stay, Michael. Step away. Stay.'
jokes.setup: Michael is being confronted by the office for spreading gossip and seeks an escape
jokes.punchline: He attempts to mount what is implied to be a manure-related vehicle/device as an escape; the chorus of 'Stay, Michael' (as if he's a dog) encapsulates the office's relationship with him perfectly
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Michael trying to mount something to escape is enhanced by the group dynamic — the 'Stay, Michael' commands are a great collective reaction beat that positions Michael as a poorly-trained pet. Solid physical comedy.

jokes.text: Michael confesses he made everything up, then adds: 'People have been saying I'm a J.Crew model.' / Others: 'We heard that about Jim.' / Michael: 'No, no, I spread the rumor that somebody was a J.Crew model and I was referring to myself.'
jokes.setup: Michael is confessing to making up all the rumors, listing them as if he's a victim too
jokes.punchline: His own 'bad rumor' turns out to be a vanity rumor about himself being a model — and even that backfired because people assumed it was about Jim (who is more conventionally attractive)
jokes.explanation: A deeply character-specific joke. Michael's 'bad rumor' is actually a good rumor about himself — he thinks being called a model is potentially harmful to his dignity, and nobody can figure out why it's bad. The kicker that Jim naturally received credit for the compliment is a perfect humiliation for Michael. The explanation 'models, even though they're very attractive, are somewhat vapid' is perfectly delusional.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Okay, I made it all up.' Andy: 'Even the fact that I'm gay?' Michael: 'Yes. Yes!' Andy: 'YES!'
jokes.setup: Michael confesses to making up all the rumors
jokes.punchline: Andy's urgent question — 'Even the fact that I'm gay?' — and his ecstatic 'YES!' celebration when confirmed
jokes.explanation: Andy's desperate need for the gay rumor to be false — and his relief when it is — is funny because we've just watched him spend several minutes convincing himself it might be true. The 'YES!' of relief lands as both funny and slightly sad given what we know. Good payoff to the Andy arc.

jokes.text: Michael: 'It's set our industry back quite a bit.' — referring to the modeling industry's reputation for vapidness
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining why being called a model could be seen as a bad rumor
jokes.punchline: He refers to modeling as 'our industry' — positioning himself as a serious stakeholder in the modeling world — with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: A small but very funny extension of the J.Crew joke. 'Our industry' implies Michael has a legitimate stake in modeling, which he absolutely does not. The confidence is what sells it.

jokes.text: Michael reveals the one true rumor: 'That Pam's pregnant.' Dwight: 'I knew it!' / 'Her breasts were a tiny bit bigger. At first I thought, oh! She has a new bra with padding. But then I thought, Pam doesn't need padding. It just didn't add up, Jim.'
jokes.setup: Michael reveals the one true rumor among all the false ones he spread
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately confirms he deduced the pregnancy from monitoring Pam's breast size — stated clinically and directly, with 'Pam doesn't need padding' delivered as a genuine compliment to Jim
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Dwight behavior — he has been monitoring his coworkers' physical attributes for deviation from baseline. 'Pam doesn't need padding' as a sincere compliment delivered to her fiancé is perfectly inappropriate in a Dwight-specific way. High character integration.

jokes.text: Michael's stream of questions when learning Pam is pregnant: 'Don't vaccinate it.' / 'Who's the father?' / 'How far along?' / 'Who's the OB-GYN?'
jokes.setup: The office is excitedly reacting to learning Pam is genuinely pregnant
jokes.punchline: 'Don't vaccinate it' lands first — Michael's anti-vax position as parenting advice — followed by 'Who's the father?' (Jim is right there), creating a rapid-fire sequence of Michael's inappropriate reactions
jokes.explanation: Great rapid-fire reaction sequence. 'Don't vaccinate it' is a perfectly bizarre opener. 'Who's the father?' when Jim is standing right there is classic Michael obliviousness. Each question is a new Michael failing.

jokes.text: Pam shows the ultrasound to prove the pregnancy. Michael: 'That is the inside of your vagina.' Jim: 'That's not how it works but...'
jokes.setup: Pam and Jim share the ultrasound as proof of the pregnancy
jokes.punchline: Michael describes the ultrasound image as 'the inside of your vagina' — anatomically wrong, socially mortifying — and Jim's dry correction 'that's not how it works' is the perfect reaction
jokes.explanation: Michael's literal, clinical, and wrong identification of the ultrasound is a great cringe beat. Jim's gentle correction maintains his role as the audience's surrogate — embarrassed but measured. The line 'it's clear why we were trying not to tell people' as a button is a good self-aware close.

jokes.text: Michael's follow-up to Jim and Pam: 'You should have told me. You're right. We should have realized that you are an equal part of this.'
jokes.setup: Michael is upset that Jim and Pam didn't tell him about the pregnancy
jokes.punchline: Pam appears to sincerely validate Michael's feelings — 'We should have realized you are an equal part of this' — which is both absurd (Michael is their boss, not a co-parent) and a perfect encapsulation of how Michael needs to be included in everything
jokes.explanation: A softer character beat. The joke is that Pam says something kind to manage Michael, and the absurdity is Michael genuinely believing he's an 'equal part' of his employees' pregnancy. More thematic than laugh-out-loud funny.

jokes.text: Michael: 'How long have you known about the pregnancy? A week? A month? A year?' Jim: 'Michael, we only told our parents last week.' Michael: 'Did you pee on a stick?' Pam: 'I did. But it was inconclusive.'
jokes.setup: Michael is emotionally processing being left out of the pregnancy news
jokes.punchline: Michael asks 'did you pee on a stick?' — both a reasonable pregnancy question and a slightly undignified one to ask a coworker — then Pam's 'it was inconclusive' as if this is additional useful information
jokes.explanation: 'Did you pee on a stick?' is intrusive but earnest. 'It was inconclusive' is a nice small absurdist beat — presumably it was conclusive enough to indicate pregnancy, so Pam's framing is oddly evasive or perhaps a reference to a first test that failed.

jokes.text: Michael has called Stanley's wife Teri to verify Stanley's story — 'Michael, Teri Hudson returning your call.'
jokes.setup: Michael promised Stanley he would say nothing
jokes.punchline: Michael has already called Stanley's wife — revealed by her returning his call — immediately undermining the promise he made thirty minutes ago
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of Michael's fundamental inability to keep secrets or promises. The timing of Teri's call is a perfect dramatic beat — Michael's betrayal is revealed mid-congratulations. The panic from Jim and Pam sells it.

jokes.text: Michael's plan to handle Teri's call: 'I'm going to tell her I need to redecorate my condo and need her help. We will haggle about money, and I will back down, and then I won't talk to her until this whole Cynthia thing has blown over.'
jokes.setup: Michael needs to talk to Teri without revealing anything about Stanley's affair
jokes.punchline: His plan is an elaborate fake interior decorating consultation — with a fully plotted arc of negotiation and backing down — that has zero chance of working and entirely misses the point of what Teri wants to know
jokes.explanation: Michael's plans are always this elaborately wrong. The specificity of 'we will haggle about money and I will back down' is funny — he's scripted a multi-act cover story. Jim and Pam's reactions ('Sounds terrible') are the right response.

jokes.text: Michael answers the phone: 'Hey, what up, Cynthia?' — calling Teri 'Cynthia,' the name of Stanley's mistress
jokes.setup: Michael is about to execute his elaborate plan to speak with Teri, Stanley's wife, without revealing the affair
jokes.punchline: He immediately calls Teri 'Cynthia' — the name of the mistress — in his very first word to her, catastrophically blowing everything at 'hello'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The setup is meticulous: Michael has an elaborate cover story, Jim and Pam are anxiously advising him not to, and he confidently takes the call. The punchline is a single word — 'Cynthia' — which destroys the entire scheme in his very first syllable. The economy is unmatched: everything collapses in one word. It's structurally perfect, character-perfect (only Michael would do this), and earns enormous impact from everything that preceded it. One of the great Michael Scott moments.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head explaining the Stanley affair outcome: 'And quite frankly, I don't think you should ever even try.' — about stopping love, after having accidentally blown up Stanley's second affair secret in one phone call
jokes.setup: Michael narrates how his phone call caused Teri to figure out Stanley's affair was ongoing
jokes.punchline: He ends the story with a philosophical endorsement of not stopping love — while being entirely responsible for exposing the affair — framing his own catastrophic blunder as a romantic act
jokes.explanation: Michael's ability to narrate his own disasters as wisdom is a running character trait. 'You can't stop love' as the moral he draws from accidentally destroying a marriage's second chance is perfectly self-serving and oblivious.

jokes.text: Intern exit interviews: 'I learned that a ream of paper is 300 sheets. I thought it was 500.' / 'Oh!'
jokes.setup: Interns are sharing what they learned from their summer
jokes.punchline: One intern's key learning is that a ream of paper is 300 sheets — which is wrong (it is 500) — and the other intern's 'Oh!' suggests they are equally surprised by the wrong fact
jokes.explanation: A quietly great joke. The intern announces wrong information (a ream is 500 sheets) as their learning, and their colleague's 'Oh!' confirms they've both internalized the false fact. It's a micro-comedy about how bad information propagates — thematically perfect for the gossip episode. The show trusts the audience to know the real answer.

jokes.text: Intern: 'I guess I didn't learn anything.' — after realizing a ream is actually 500 sheets
jokes.setup: The intern confidently stated that a ream is 300 sheets as their key learning
jokes.punchline: Upon realizing it's actually 500, the immediate philosophical conclusion is 'I guess I didn't learn anything' — total epistemological collapse in five words
jokes.explanation: Excellent button. The logic is impeccably absurd: the intern's entire summer is retroactively invalidated because one fact was wrong. Economy is near-perfect. 'I guess I didn't learn anything' is the comedic equivalent of a single perfect mic drop.

jokes.text: Intern: 'I learned that if you look even the tiniest bit like Jet Li, Michael will call you Jet Li all summer.' / Michael: 'Julia Stiles. Alan Thicke.'
jokes.setup: Interns are sharing what they learned; one references being called 'Jet Li' all summer by Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael, with no shame, immediately demonstrates the behavior by miscalling two other interns by celebrity names (Julia Stiles, Alan Thicke) — proving the point in real time
jokes.explanation: A superb closing joke. The structure is perfect: intern complains about being called Jet Li, Michael demonstrates the habit immediately with two new names. The specific celebrities chosen are funny in themselves — 'Alan Thicke' as a celebrity Michael would name-check is perfect, and 'Julia Stiles' is equally specific and wrong. The joke works on multiple levels: it's about Michael's racism (veiled behind celebrity association), his obliviousness, and the interns' resigned acceptance. One of the episode's strongest.

tmdb_overview: A few interns who stayed at Dunder-Mifflin over the summer end their internship. Michael announces some potentially damaging gossip about an employee to the rest of the office, then starts to spread false rumours about others to cover up what he has unwittingly revealed.
